questions.question: New Mexico is called the Land of Enchantment largely because of its:
questions.correctAnswer: Dramatic high-desert landscapes, mountains and wide skies
distractors: Tropical beaches and ocean ports
Flat farmland in every direction
Year-round heavy rainfall
questions.explanation: New Mexico is a high, dry state of deserts, mesas and mountain ranges under huge skies. The Land of Enchantment nickname, adopted officially in 1999, points to that scenery and to the mix of cultures layered into it.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Enchantment means desert, mesas and mountains - not beaches.

questions.question: The river that flows the full length of New Mexico from north to south is the:
questions.correctAnswer: Rio Grande
distractors: Colorado River
Pecos River
Canadian River
questions.explanation: The Rio Grande enters New Mexico near the Colorado line, runs through Taos, Albuquerque and Las Cruces, and forms the border with Texas at El Paso. Farms, cities and Pueblos have depended on its water for centuries.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Rio Grande is New Mexico's north-to-south lifeline.

img.tip: T-Rexy says: The Rio Grande is New Mexico's north-to-south lifeline.

questions.question: Santa Fe, the capital of New Mexico, sits at the foot of which mountains?
questions.correctAnswer: The Sangre de Cristo Mountains
distractors: The Sandia Mountains
The Sacramento Mountains
The Gila Mountains
questions.explanation: Santa Fe lies about 7,000 feet above sea level at the southern end of the Sangre de Cristo range, the southernmost Rockies in New Mexico. That elevation makes it the highest state capital in the United States.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Santa Fe sits high, under the Sangre de Cristos.

img.scene: An adobe city at the foot of a high pine-covered mountain range, late light on flat roofs. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Santa Fe sits high, under the Sangre de Cristos.
img.title: SANTA FE AND THE MOUNTAINS

questions.question: In the five themes of geography, studying how the Rio Grande bosque and desert plants fit their dry home is an example of:
questions.correctAnswer: Human-environment interaction and region
distractors: Location - latitude and longitude only
Movement - trade routes only
Place names and map symbols
questions.explanation: Geographers use location, place, human-environment interaction, movement and region. Plants, animals and people adapting to scarce water - and people changing the river with dams and ditches - is human-environment interaction inside a desert region.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Dry-land adaptation is human-environment interaction at work.

img.scene: Irrigation ditches carrying river water into green fields beside a dry desert plain, mountains behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Dry-land adaptation is human-environment interaction at work.
img.title: FIVE THEMES IN NEW MEXICO

questions.question: Most of New Mexico's fresh water for cities and farms comes from:
questions.correctAnswer: Snowmelt in the mountains, stored in rivers, reservoirs and aquifers
distractors: Ocean desalination plants
Heavy summer rainfall alone
Water piped from the Great Lakes
questions.explanation: New Mexico is arid, so water is the state's most contested resource. Mountain snowpack feeds the Rio Grande and other rivers; reservoirs store it, acequias and canals deliver it, and wells tap underground aquifers.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In New Mexico, water starts as mountain snow.

img.scene: Snow-covered peaks above a blue reservoir, an irrigation canal leading toward farm fields below. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: In New Mexico, water starts as mountain snow.
img.title: WATER IS LIFE HERE

questions.question: New Mexico's four geographic regions include high plains in the east and which landform dominating the center and west?
questions.correctAnswer: Basins and ranges with mesas and desert valleys
distractors: A coastal plain along an ocean
A single flat prairie with no mountains
Glacier-covered lowlands
questions.explanation: The state divides roughly into mountains in the north and center, the Basin and Range country of the south and west, the high plains of the east, and the Colorado Plateau in the northwest. Elevation, not rainfall alone, shapes each region's life.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mountains, basins, plains, plateau - four New Mexico worlds.

img.scene: A sweeping view across desert basins, flat-topped mesas and distant mountain ranges under a huge sky. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Mountains, basins, plains, plateau - four New Mexico worlds.
img.title: FOUR REGIONS, ONE STATE

questions.question: Why do temperatures in Albuquerque swing so much between a summer afternoon and the same night?
questions.correctAnswer: Dry desert air and high elevation let heat escape quickly after sunset
distractors: Ocean breezes cool the city every night
The mountains block all sunlight by 4 p.m.
Summer nights bring desert snowstorms
questions.explanation: Dry air holds little moisture, so it heats fast by day and cools fast at night. Albuquerque sits over a mile high, which sharpens the swing. Big day-night temperature changes are a signature of high-desert climate.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Dry air heats fast and cools fast - expect the swing.

img.scene: A desert city at dusk, warm orange light fading over rooftops with cool blue mountains behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Dry air heats fast and cools fast - expect the swing.
img.title: HOT DAYS, COOL NIGHTS

questions.question: A geographer drawing the boundary between New Mexico's farm belt and its desert rangeland is mainly mapping a difference in:
questions.correctAnswer: How people use land shaped by water availability
distractors: Time zones
State voting districts only
Mountain heights alone
questions.explanation: Land use follows water. Irrigated valleys along rivers support farms and towns, while dry uplands support cattle ranching over large areas. Mapping that contrast shows human choices responding to a scarce resource.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Farms follow water; ranches spread across the dry land.

img.scene: Green irrigated fields in a river valley giving way to dry golden rangeland and mesas beyond. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Farms follow water; ranches spread across the dry land.
img.title: FARMS FOLLOW WATER

questions.question: Which statement best explains why so many New Mexico settlements - Pueblos, Spanish towns and later cities - grew along rivers?
questions.correctAnswer: In an arid land, permanent settlement requires dependable water for drinking, farming and stock
distractors: Rivers were the only land the law allowed anyone to settle
Desert land cannot support any buildings
Settlers avoided mountains for religious reasons in every era
questions.explanation: From Ancestral Pueblo farmers to Spanish colonists to modern cities, settlement in New Mexico clusters where water is reliable. The Rio Grande and Pecos valleys hold most of the population for exactly that reason.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No water, no town - New Mexico history follows its rivers.

img.scene: An adobe village beside a green river corridor, desert and mesas stretching empty beyond the trees. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No water, no town - New Mexico history follows its rivers.
img.title: TOWNS FOLLOW RIVERS

questions.question: New Mexico shares its Four Corners point with which three states?
questions.correctAnswer: Arizona, Colorado and Utah
distractors: Arizona, Texas and Oklahoma
Colorado, Kansas and Texas
Utah, Nevada and Arizona
questions.explanation: At the Four Corners Monument, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah meet at a single point - the only place in the United States where four states touch. The point sits in the Colorado Plateau country of the northwest.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Four Corners: New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Utah.

img.scene: Four state boundary lines meeting at one point on a desert plateau, mesas in the distance. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Four Corners: New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Utah.
img.title: FOUR CORNERS

questions.question: The fluted spear points first found near the town of Folsom showed that:
questions.correctAnswer: People hunted giant Ice Age bison in New Mexico about 10,000 years ago
distractors: People farmed corn in New Mexico 10,000 years ago
The first New Mexicans arrived by ship
Bison were introduced to New Mexico by Spaniards
questions.explanation: In 1908 a cowboy found huge bison bones at Folsom, and excavations in the 1920s found a stone point lodged among them. Folsom points proved people lived and hunted in the Southwest far earlier than most experts had believed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A point in the bison bones pushed New Mexico history back millennia.

img.scene: An ancient giant bison on an Ice Age grassland, distant hunters small on the horizon, storm light. No people in sharp focus. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: A point in the bison bones pushed New Mexico history back millennia.
img.title: THE FOLSOM DISCOVERY

questions.question: Clovis points, named for finds near Clovis, New Mexico, are evidence of:
questions.correctAnswer: Early Paleoindian hunters who stalked mammoths and other big game
distractors: Spanish colonial soldiers
Pueblo farmers of the 1400s
Apache raiders of the 1800s
questions.explanation: Clovis culture, dated to roughly 13,000 years ago, is named for the New Mexico town where its large fluted points were recognized in the 1930s. Clovis hunters pursued mammoths and giant bison across a cooler, wetter Southwest.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Clovis, New Mexico gave an Ice Age culture its name.

img.scene: A mammoth on a cold grassland with shallow lakes, fluted stone points resting on a rock in the foreground. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Clovis, New Mexico gave an Ice Age culture its name.
img.title: CLOVIS HUNTERS

questions.question: As the Ice Age ended and the climate grew warmer and drier, early New Mexicans adapted by:
questions.correctAnswer: Hunting smaller game and gathering a wider range of wild plants
distractors: Building large stone cities right away
Leaving the region empty for thousands of years
Switching completely to ocean fishing
questions.explanation: Archaic peoples responded to warming by broadening their diet: deer, rabbits, seeds, nuts and roots, harvested with grinding stones called manos and metates. Flexible seasonal movement replaced big-game specialization.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: When the giants vanished, the menu widened.

img.scene: Hands grinding seeds on a flat stone slab beside baskets of gathered wild plants, desert hills behind. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: When the giants vanished, the menu widened.
img.title: THE ARCHAIC ADAPTATION

questions.question: Archaeologists learn about the earliest New Mexicans mainly from:
questions.correctAnswer: Artifacts, animal bones, ancient campsites and other physical remains
distractors: Written diaries kept by Paleoindians
Spanish mission records
Photographs and newspapers
questions.explanation: Peoples before writing left no documents. Archaeologists reconstruct their lives from stone tools, bones, fire hearths, pollen and settlement patterns - evidence that must be interpreted carefully and can change with new finds.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No diaries - stones, bones and ash tell the story.

img.scene: An archaeologist's grid over an ancient campsite, stone tools and pottery fragments laid out on a tray. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: No diaries - stones, bones and ash tell the story.
img.title: READING THE REMAINS

questions.question: The shift from Clovis to Folsom to later Archaic cultures in New Mexico was driven most directly by:
questions.correctAnswer: Climate change that transformed grasslands and the animals living on them
distractors: Orders from a central government
The arrival of horses from Europe
A single great war between tribes
questions.explanation: As temperatures rose and rainfall patterns shifted, mammoths and giant bison died out and plant communities changed. Each cultural shift in the sequence tracks people re-tooling their lives for a new environment.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The climate changed first; cultures changed in answer.

img.scene: A landscape split between a green Ice Age lake plain and the dry desert that replaced it. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The climate changed first; cultures changed in answer.
img.title: CLIMATE MOVED FIRST

questions.question: Sandia Cave, in the mountains east of Albuquerque, became famous because early reports claimed it held:
questions.correctAnswer: Some of the oldest human evidence in the Americas
distractors: Gold buried by Spanish explorers
The first Pueblo pottery ever made
A lost Apache treaty document
questions.explanation: Excavations at Sandia Cave in the 1930s and 1940s were announced as extremely ancient, though later scholars questioned parts of the dating. The debate itself shows how archaeology tests bold claims against evidence.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sandia Cave: a famous claim, carefully questioned.

img.scene: A dark cave mouth high in a rocky mountain canyon, a ladder of light falling across the entrance. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Sandia Cave: a famous claim, carefully questioned.
img.title: SANDIA CAVE

questions.question: Why did Paleoindian groups move often instead of settling in one village?
questions.correctAnswer: They followed migrating herds and seasonal foods across large territories
distractors: They were forbidden by law to build houses
No building materials existed anywhere in the region
They were all fleeing one permanent enemy
questions.explanation: Big-game hunting and wild-food gathering reward mobility. Small bands camped near water and game, then moved on. Permanent villages only became practical much later, once farming could feed people in one place.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Hunters move; farmers stay. The earliest New Mexicans moved.

img.scene: A small camp of hide shelters beside a stream at dawn, bundles and tools ready to carry. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Hunters move; farmers stay. The earliest New Mexicans moved.
img.title: LIFE ON THE MOVE

questions.question: A mano and metate found at an ancient New Mexico site tell archaeologists that the people there:
questions.correctAnswer: Ground seeds or corn into meal as part of food preparation
distractors: Minted coins for trade
Built with cut stone blocks
Made metal tools
questions.explanation: The metate is a flat grinding slab and the mano the handstone rubbed across it. Together they processed hard seeds - and later corn - into flour, evidence of plant foods becoming central to the diet.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Grinding stones mean plant foods mattered.

img.scene: A flat stone slab and a smooth hand stone with a small pile of ground meal beside them. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Grinding stones mean plant foods mattered.
img.title: MANO AND METATE

questions.question: Dating a Folsom site depends most on which kind of evidence?
questions.correctAnswer: Radiocarbon dates from charcoal or bone found with the artifacts
distractors: The depth of the site below the modern surface alone
Oral stories recorded in the 1900s
The opinions of the first collectors
questions.explanation: A point style alone gives only a relative age. Radiocarbon dating of associated charcoal or bone anchors sites in calendar years, which is how the roughly 10,000-year age of Folsom occupation was established.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Charcoal plus radiocarbon turns a layer into a date.

img.scene: Layers of earth in an excavation wall with charcoal flecks and a stone point visible in one band. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Charcoal plus radiocarbon turns a layer into a date.
img.title: DATING THE PAST

questions.question: The best-supported conclusion from New Mexico's Paleoindian record is that:
questions.correctAnswer: People were present in the region by the end of the last Ice Age and adapted as it warmed
distractors: People arrived only after Spanish contact
The region was uninhabited until farming began
One single group lived unchanged for 10,000 years
questions.explanation: Clovis and Folsom materials, supported by radiocarbon dates, place people in New Mexico over 10,000 years ago. Cultures then changed repeatedly - new tools, new foods, new settlement patterns - as climate and game changed.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Present early, adapting always - that is the record.

img.scene: Stone points of different shapes arranged in a row from oldest to newest against a desert backdrop. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Present early, adapting always - that is the record.
img.title: PRESENT EARLY, ADAPTING

questions.question: The farming peoples who built the great stone towns of Chaco Canyon are known today as:
questions.correctAnswer: Ancestral Pueblo people (often called Anasazi in older books)
distractors: Aztecs
Plains Sioux
Spanish colonists
questions.explanation: Ancestral Pueblo people farmed the San Juan Basin and built Chaco's great houses by the 800s-1100s CE. Modern Pueblo peoples are their descendants, and many prefer Ancestral Pueblo to the older Navajo-derived word Anasazi.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Chaco's builders were Ancestral Pueblo people.

img.scene: A great circular kiva and multi-story stone walls in a desert canyon under morning light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Chaco's builders were Ancestral Pueblo people.
img.title: ANCESTRAL PUEBLO PEOPLE

questions.question: Corn, beans and squash grown together are often called the:
questions.correctAnswer: Three Sisters
distractors: Three Rivers
Three Mountains
Three Pueblos
questions.explanation: Corn stalks give beans a pole to climb, beans add nitrogen to the soil, and squash leaves shade the ground and hold moisture. The Three Sisters package, arriving from Mexico over centuries, anchored Pueblo farming.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Corn holds, beans feed, squash shades - Three Sisters.

img.scene: Corn stalks with climbing bean vines and broad squash leaves spreading at their feet in a desert garden. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Corn holds, beans feed, squash shades - Three Sisters.
img.title: THE THREE SISTERS

questions.question: Pueblo Bonito at Chaco Canyon was remarkable because it was:
questions.correctAnswer: A great house of hundreds of rooms, among the largest buildings in North America for its time
distractors: A Spanish fort built in 1598
A natural rock formation with no rooms
A single-family farmhouse
questions.explanation: Pueblo Bonito rose four to five stories with some 600 rooms and dozens of kivas, built between about 850 and 1150 CE. Roads, timber hauled from distant mountains and trade goods like turquoise tie it to a wide regional system.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Pueblo Bonito: hundreds of rooms in the desert.

img.scene: A vast curved multi-story stone great house filling a canyon floor, ladders against its walls. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Pueblo Bonito: hundreds of rooms in the desert.
img.title: PUEBLO BONITO

questions.question: Kivas - the round ceremonial rooms of Pueblo communities - were used for:
questions.correctAnswer: Ceremonies, meetings and community gatherings, entered by ladder through the roof
distractors: Storing gunpowder for Spanish soldiers
Housing horses and cattle
Smelting iron ore
questions.explanation: Kivas descend from earlier pit houses. A ladder through the roof hatch served as the door, and the enclosed round room hosted ceremonies and council work. Kivas remain sacred, active spaces in Pueblo life today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Down the ladder, into the kiva - ceremony and council.

img.scene: A round stone ceremonial room seen from above, a wooden ladder rising through its roof opening. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Down the ladder, into the kiva - ceremony and council.
img.title: THE KIVA

questions.question: When long drought struck the Colorado Plateau in the late 1200s, many Ancestral Pueblo families responded by:
questions.correctAnswer: Migrating to the Rio Grande valley and other better-watered places
distractors: Sailing to South America
Giving up farming forever everywhere
Building taller walls at Chaco without moving
questions.explanation: Tree rings record a Great Drought from 1276 to 1299. Chaco and Mesa Verde emptied as families moved south and east - many to the Rio Grande valley, where descendant Pueblos stand today. Migration was an adaptation, not a disappearance.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Drought moved people to the river - they did not vanish.

img.scene: Families carrying bundles along a trail from dry cliff dwellings toward a green river valley far below. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Drought moved people to the river - they did not vanish.
img.title: THE GREAT MIGRATION

questions.question: The Rio Grande valley Pueblos farmed successfully in a dry land mainly by:
questions.correctAnswer: Irrigating fields with river water through ditches
distractors: Waiting for daily rain
Farming only in mountain snowfields
Importing all food from Mexico
questions.explanation: River irrigation turned valley bottoms into reliable farmland. Communal labor dug and cleaned ditches, and water sharing was organized by the community - a system Spanish colonists later adopted as the acequia.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ditches from the river made valley farming reliable.

img.scene: Earthen irrigation ditches carrying river water between green corn fields beside adobe homes. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Ditches from the river made valley farming reliable.
img.title: RIVER IRRIGATION

questions.question: Turquoise, shell and macaw feathers found at Chaco show that its people:
questions.correctAnswer: Traded across long distances reaching into Mexico
distractors: Never left their own canyon
Mined turquoise only for local use
Received goods as gifts from Spanish explorers
questions.explanation: Chaco held turquoise workshops, Gulf and Pacific shells, copper bells and live macaws from far to the south. Such goods could only arrive through trade networks spanning hundreds of miles.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Macaws and shells in the desert mean long-distance trade.

img.scene: Turquoise stones, white shells and bright feathers arranged on a woven blanket in canyon light. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Macaws and shells in the desert mean long-distance trade.
img.title: TRADE FROM FAR AWAY

questions.question: The Mogollon peoples of southwestern New Mexico are especially known for:
questions.correctAnswer: Mimbres pottery painted with bold black-on-white designs of animals and people
distractors: Building the Chaco great houses
Introducing horses to the Plains
Writing the first New Mexico laws
questions.explanation: Mimbres potters of the Mimbres Valley created some of the finest painted pottery in the ancient Southwest - bowls showing fish, birds, animals and human figures, dating roughly 1000-1150 CE.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Mimbres bowls: black paint, white clay, living figures.

img.scene: Black-on-white painted bowls with stylized birds and animals, resting on a woven mat. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Mimbres bowls: black paint, white clay, living figures.
img.title: MIMBRES POTTERY

questions.question: Athabaskan-speaking peoples who migrated into the Southwest by about the 1400s-1500s became the ancestors of today's:
questions.correctAnswer: Navajo (Dine) and Apache peoples
distractors: Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande
Spanish settlers of Santa Fe
Mimbres potters
questions.explanation: Navajo and Apache languages belong to the Athabaskan family, whose other speakers live far north in Canada and Alaska. Their ancestors moved south over generations, then built distinct Southwestern cultures - farming, raiding, trading and adapting.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Navajo and Apache roots reach north to Athabaskan country.

img.scene: A hogan and a tipi-shaped shelter on open land between mesas, evening light, no figures in focus. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Navajo and Apache roots reach north to Athabaskan country.
img.title: ATHABASKAN ARRIVALS

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say the Ancestral Pueblo people simply disappeared?
questions.correctAnswer: Their descendants live in today's Pueblos, and migration - not extinction - emptied the old centers
distractors: They left written records saying they vanished
Every old site was destroyed by volcanoes
They all became Spanish citizens in 1598
questions.explanation: Pueblo oral histories describe migrations to present homelands, and archaeology, language and living culture connect Chaco and Mesa Verde to modern Pueblos. The great houses were left behind; the people continued.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The people moved. The Pueblos are their living proof.

img.scene: An ancient great house in one view and a living adobe Pueblo village with ladders and ovens in another. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: The people moved. The Pueblos are their living proof.
img.title: THE PEOPLE CONTINUED

questions.question: In 1540, Francisco Vasquez de Coronado's expedition came to the Pueblos searching for:
questions.correctAnswer: The rumored wealthy cities of Cibola
distractors: A sea route to India through the desert
Coal deposits for Spanish ships
The headwaters of the Mississippi River
questions.explanation: Reports of golden cities drew Coronado north from Mexico with hundreds of soldiers and Indigenous allies. At the Zuni Pueblos - the real Cibola - he found adobe towns and corn, not gold, then wintered at Tiguex near today's Bernalillo.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Coronado chased golden Cibola and found corn towns.

img.scene: Armored Spanish riders on a desert trail approaching adobe Pueblo buildings under a huge sky, distant view. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Coronado chased golden Cibola and found corn towns.
img.title: CORONADO'S SEARCH

questions.question: Esteban, an enslaved North African scout sent ahead of the Spanish entrada, reached the Zuni area in 1539 and is remembered because he:
questions.correctAnswer: Was the first known African and non-Indigenous outsider to reach the Pueblos
distractors: Founded the city of Santa Fe
Signed the first treaty with the Navajo
Brought the first horses to breed in New Mexico
questions.explanation: Esteban (Estevanico) traveled ahead of Fray Marcos de Niza in 1539 and was killed at the Zuni Pueblo of Hawikuh. His reports - and the friar's - helped launch Coronado's expedition the next year.
questions.memoryHook: Esteban walked first into Pueblo country in 1539.

img.scene: A lone traveler with a gourd rattle crossing a desert valley toward a distant adobe pueblo at dawn. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Esteban walked first into Pueblo country in 1539.
img.title: ESTEBAN THE SCOUT

questions.question: Coronado's men wintering at Tiguex in 1540-41 caused lasting harm mainly by:
questions.correctAnswer: Demanding food, clothing and shelter from the Pueblos, which sparked the Tiguex War
distractors: Teaching the Pueblos to irrigate
Building the first public schools
Freeing all Pueblo captives
questions.explanation: Requisitioning supplies in winter pushed the Tiguex Pueblos to resist; Spanish forces stormed pueblos and burned captives. The violence of 1540-42 became a remembered warning when settlers returned sixty years later.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Winter demands at Tiguex turned hosts into enemies.

img.scene: Snow on adobe rooftops, Spanish soldiers carrying away sacks of corn while Pueblo families watch from doorways, distant view. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: Winter demands at Tiguex turned hosts into enemies.
img.title: THE TIGUEX WAR

questions.question: A Pueblo guide the Spanish called El Turco led Coronado onto the plains of Kansas and later admitted he had:
questions.correctAnswer: Invented tales of rich Quivira, apparently hoping the expedition would get lost or turn back
distractors: Hidden a working gold mine near Santa Fe
Drawn the first accurate map of the Rio Grande
Converted the expedition to Pueblo religion
questions.explanation: Hoping to mislead the strangers who had seized Pueblo supplies, the guide described wealthy Quivira far to the east. Coronado found grass-house villages and no gold, and the guide paid with his life - an early act of Indigenous resistance.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A false golden trail was itself a weapon of resistance.

img.scene: An endless grass sea under a vast sky, a small expedition column dwarfed by the plains. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: T-Rexy says: A false golden trail was itself a weapon of resistance.
img.title: THE GUIDE'S GAMBIT

questions.question: The Rodriguez-Chamuscado (1581) and Espejo (1582) expeditions mattered to Spain mainly because they:
questions.correctAnswer: Renewed reports of settled Pueblo peoples and possible mines, preparing the way for colonization
distractors: Founded permanent Spanish towns in New Mexico

questions.question: Comparing the Spanish entry (1598) with the American entry (1846), the sharpest difference is:
questions.correctAnswer: Spain colonized slowly with settlers, missions and tribute over centuries; the United States annexed by war and treaty at once, then argued for 62 years over statehood
distractors: Spain arrived by treaty after a war; the United States arrived with missions
Neither power made any promises to the people already living there
Both entries were welcomed unanimously by all New Mexicans
questions.explanation: Onate brought families to stay and a mission system to transform; Kearny brought an army, a legal code and a treaty that transferred sovereignty in a signature. Both made promises - about land, faith and rights - whose keeping New Mexicans still measure.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Settlers and missions versus army and treaty: two entries, two logics.
